title: Settersten & Godlewski (2016): Multiple Choice
instructions: Choose the single answer that most accurately reflects the chapter.

items.prompt: Which pair captures the chapter's two main strands of inquiry?
options: Biological and pathological aging as processes confined to an individual organism
Age as a property of individuals and groups, and of social organization and dynamics
Childhood development and late-life decline as one fixed sequence of cognitive stages
Qualitative and quantitative methods ranked by their general scientific superiority
items.answer: Age as a property of individuals and groups, and of social organization and dynamics
items.explanation: The chapter contrasts individual-level proxies, time, and subjective experiences with social phases, norms, institutions, and intersections.

items.prompt: What should researchers ask when including chronological age in an analysis?
options: Is this sample older than every sample used in previous research?
Which age cutoffs make the group differences statistically significant?
What process does age represent, and can that process be measured directly?
Has age been included automatically as a control?
items.answer: What process does age represent, and can that process be measured directly?
items.explanation: Age is not itself the underlying mechanism. Researchers must theorize the psychological, social, biological, or functional process it indexes.

items.prompt: Which is NOT an example of relative personal time?
options: Being 53 when a daughter graduates
Retiring at 67 after 40 years as a professor
Having children three years apart
Assuming all 67-year-olds have identical functional ability
items.answer: Assuming all 67-year-olds have identical functional ability
items.explanation: The first three describe time to an event, time in a role, or time between events. The final option assumes within-age homogeneity.

items.prompt: Which interpretation is necessary for awareness of age-related change?
options: Attributing every change to illness
Attributing personal changes to somebody else's aging
Treating all changes as random events
Attributing perceived changes to one's own increasing chronological age
items.answer: Attributing perceived changes to one's own increasing chronological age
items.explanation: AARC includes conscious perceptions of change and attribution to increased chronological age rather than other conditions.

items.prompt: Which distinction between age and cohort explanations is accurate?
options: Age concerns maturation; cohort concerns historical events and social change
Age concerns only historical change; cohort concerns only biological maturation
Age and cohort are always interchangeable explanations
Both refer only to generational positions inside a family
items.answer: Age concerns maturation; cohort concerns historical events and social change
items.explanation: Age and cohort index lifetime and historical time respectively. Using them without distinguishing the underlying processes confuses the explanation.

items.prompt: Why may family life be less age-structured than economic and political life?
options: Families have no life phases, generations, or role transitions
Family relationships operate independently of laws, markets, and welfare systems
Family time is less linear, and bodily and others' needs constrain planning
Family members generally do not know their chronological ages
items.answer: Family time is less linear, and bodily and others' needs constrain planning
items.explanation: Illness, childbirth, and childrearing needs can resist predictable clock-time schedules and contribute to work–family time conflicts.

items.prompt: What was the original purpose of Neugarten's young-old/old-old distinction?
options: To prescribe different social-security eligibility rules for two fixed ages
To establish ages 65 and 75 as universal biological boundaries
To divide people in their twenties into fixed categories of old age
To distinguish health, affluence, and activity regardless of chronological age
items.answer: To distinguish health, affluence, and activity regardless of chronological age
items.explanation: The original concepts emphasized heterogeneity among people of the same age, rather than the fixed age bands adopted later.

items.prompt: Which statement about age stereotypes matches the chapter?
options: Only negative stereotypes have social consequences
Positive stereotypes may provide advantages while also creating unrealistic standards
Younger people cannot be targets of ageism
Ageism is experienced identically across gender and racial groups
items.answer: Positive stereotypes may provide advantages while also creating unrealistic standards
items.explanation: The authors call for study of positive stereotypes while warning that overly positive portrayals of successful aging may be unattainable for many people.

items.prompt: Which pairing describes what age norms provide and how conformity is enforced?
options: Randomness and unpredictability; complete social indifference to deviation
Order and predictability; sanctions through rewards and penalties
Biological immutability; genetic testing
Historical sameness; removal of cohort differences
items.answer: Order and predictability; sanctions through rewards and penalties
items.explanation: Age scripts organize lives, while social sanctions can reward staying on track or penalize departures from expected timing.

items.prompt: What is the authors' position on age integration and segregation?
options: Both involve costs and benefits that require attention to context
Mixing age groups automatically eliminates every intergenerational conflict
Age-restricted communities arise only through coercion
Intergenerational relationships outside the family are unimportant
items.answer: Both involve costs and benefits that require attention to context
items.explanation: Age-diverse networks may bring conflict as well as cooperation; restricted communities may provide peer relationships and health-related support.

items.prompt: What underlies the concentration of US social programs in early and later life?
options: Assumptions about risk and dependence in childhood and old age
A framework designed exclusively to fund education for middle-aged adults
Identical benefits for everyone regardless of age, need, or circumstances
A policy requiring every older person to work until death
items.answer: Assumptions about risk and dependence in childhood and old age
items.explanation: The chapter describes protection and investment for children, and health and economic security and feasible retirement for older adults.

items.prompt: Which example illustrates a gendered double standard of aging?
options: Visible aging always increases social capital equally for men and women
Visible aging invariably increases only women's social capital
Signs of aging may add to men's social capital while diminishing women's
Cultural meanings have no bearing on evaluations of aging bodies
items.answer: Signs of aging may add to men's social capital while diminishing women's
items.explanation: Treating aging as a gender-neutral phenomenon conceals differences in the meanings, expectations, and evaluations attached to age.

items.prompt: Which was NOT one of the three meanings of age examined in Project AGE?
options: Cognitive meaning
Evaluative meaning
Social participation and interaction norms
Genetic meaning
items.explanation: The study compared perceived age categories, the values attached to ages, and norms governing interaction across age groups.

items.prompt: What is needed to interpret age-group differences as evidence about maturation?
options: More finely divided age bands that automatically reveal individual change
Relabeling every observed difference as a cohort effect
Treating the coefficient of an automatic age control as a cause
A theory identifying the processes that produce the observed age differences
items.answer: A theory identifying the processes that produce the observed age differences
items.explanation: Stacking age groups into an artificial growth curve can confuse individual change with cohort differences. Theory must identify the relevant mechanisms.

items.prompt: Which statement best captures the chapter's concluding paradox?
options: Age directly causes every individual change, so social institutions are irrelevant
A science without age makes institutions unnecessary to study
Understanding aging may require moving beyond age, even though social age remains consequential
Gerontology should study only chronological age
items.answer: Understanding aging may require moving beyond age, even though social age remains consequential
items.explanation: The conclusion holds together the critique of age as an individual-level proxy and its substantial consequences as a principle of social organization.
